prompt.context: Your client is a rich financier who has decided recently to enter the capital markets as a market maker. Market makers make % commissions off of transactions in capital markets, and are necessary to provide liquidity and orderly market action. The year is 2014 and he believes that we have recovered long enough from the financial collapse to warrant an investment in this sector. There are multiple opportunities in the financial market and you have been hired to advise him on how and where to invest his money. He is considering entry into one of four markets: Commodities, Options, Equities, and Fixed Income.
prompt.question: Which of the four markets — Commodities, Options, Equities, or Fixed Income — should the client enter as a market maker, and why?

clarifying_info.q: How much capital is available to invest?
Does the client have trading experience?
clarifying_info.a: He has experience in finance, but not specifically in trading.
Investment to be focused inside the United States.

clarifying_info.q: What is the financial goal and can he invest in multiple markets?
clarifying_info.a: Goal is a positive NPV investment. He is limited to only one investment — he feels his attention can only be focused on one opportunity at a time.

clarifying_info.q: Can you share the size and market shares of the four markets?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — see Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2 (handed to candidate after initial structuring).

clarifying_info.q: How do market makers earn money?
clarifying_info.a: Market makers make a fixed % commission on each transaction, so more volume and higher $ value of transactions is generally better. Each market has intrinsically different commission rates, which are not available.

exhibits.title: Market Size and Transaction Volume
exhibits.shows: Two side-by-side bar charts comparing the four markets: (1) Total assets in market ($trillion) and (2) Number of transactions (millions/year) for Commodities, Options, Equities, and Fixed Income.
exhibits.data: Chart 1 — Total assets ($T): Fixed Income largest, then Equities, then Options, then Commodities (smallest). Chart 2 — Number of transactions (millions/yr): Options and Commodities highest (roughly 1,000 and 900+), Equities and Fixed Income lower (roughly 300-400).

exhibits.title: Competitive Landscape
exhibits.shows: A table or chart showing the number and relative size of market participants (players) in each of the four markets. A note states that Player 2 in the Equities market recently had a rogue trader incident and is looking to exit through asset liquidation.
exhibits.data: Commodities: fewer major players. Options and Fixed Income: dominated by a few large players. Equities: Player 2 is seeking to liquidate assets and exit. Note: '*Player 2 in the Equities market recently had a rogue trader incident and is looking to exit through asset liquidation.'

exhibits.title: Expected P&L and Investment ($MM)
exhibits.shows: An income-statement-style table with rows for Expected Revenue, Salaries, Rent & Utilities, Depreciation, Operating Profit, Interest Expense, Earnings Before Tax, Taxes, Net Income, and Expected Investment across the four markets. Several cells are missing (marked '??'). Cost of capital = 5%; all income assumed to last forever beginning in Year 1; depreciation is constant year-over-year.
exhibits.data: Commodities: Revenue=200, Salaries=50, Rent=50, Depreciation=??, OperatingProfit=60, InterestExp=30, EBT=30, Taxes=10, NetIncome=20, Investment=2000. Options: Revenue=??, Salaries=40, Rent=40, Depreciation=30, OperatingProfit=70, InterestExp=20, EBT=50, Taxes=10, NetIncome=40, Investment=2500. Equities: Revenue=150, Salaries=20, Rent=40, Depreciation=25, OperatingProfit=65, InterestExp=20, EBT=45, Taxes=??, NetIncome=30, Investment=1500. FixedIncome: Revenue=160, Salaries=30, Rent=30, Depreciation=50, OperatingProfit=??, InterestExp=40, EBT=10, Taxes=2, NetIncome=8, Investment=2100.

framework: Understand the market-maker business model: revenue = % commission × transaction volume × transaction size
Segment analysis: assess each of the four markets on size (assets), volume (transactions), and competitive dynamics
Financial analysis: fill in missing P&L cells, compute EBITDA, perform perpetuity-based NPV for each market
Synthesize: rank markets by NPV and qualitative attractiveness, select the one positive-NPV option
Recommendation with risks and next steps

questions.prompt: From Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2, which markets look most attractive before running the numbers?
questions.guidance: Strong answer integrates both charts and the competitive note. High transaction volume (Options, Commodities) is good for a commission-based business. High total assets (Fixed Income, Equities) also matter. Commodities has fewer major players (easier entry). Equities has a distressed seller (cheap entry opportunity). Options and Fixed Income are dominated by a few large players (hard to enter). Candidate should note that no exhibit shows actual profit, so NPV analysis is still required.

questions.prompt: Fill in the missing cells in Exhibit 3 and compute NPV for each market. Cost of capital is 5% and all income lasts forever.
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize EBITDA = Operating Profit + Depreciation (since Depreciation is non-cash). Investment return = EBITDA / 0.05 (perpetuity formula). NPV = Investment Return − Expected Investment. Top candidates recognize that Net Income is a distractor and only EBITDA and Investment are needed for NPV. Candidate should also correctly back-solve the four missing cells.

math.setup: Step 1: Back-solve missing cells. Step 2: EBITDA = Operating Profit + Depreciation. Step 3: Investment Return = EBITDA / cost-of-capital (perpetuity: CF/r). Step 4: NPV = Investment Return − Expected Investment.
steps: Missing cells: Commodities Depreciation = Revenue(200) − Salaries(50) − Rent(50) − OperatingProfit(60) = 40
Options Revenue = Salaries(40) + Rent(40) + Depreciation(30) + OperatingProfit(70) = 180
Fixed Income Operating Profit = Revenue(160) − Salaries(30) − Rent(30) − Depreciation(50) = 50
Investment Return (EBITDA/0.05): Commodities=2000; Options=2000; Equities=1800; FixedIncome=2000
math.answer: Only Equities has a positive NPV (+$300MM). Commodities is breakeven (NPV=0). Options and Fixed Income are negative. Equities is the only viable investment.

questions.prompt: Given the NPV results, which market should the client enter?
questions.guidance: Equities is the only positive-NPV option (+$300MM). The cheap entry cost is enabled by Player 2's distressed asset liquidation. An added benefit is that the $1.5B investment leaves ~$1B of the $2.5B budget free for other uses. Candidate may note this but it is not required.

recommendation: Invest in the Equities market as a market maker at an expected investment of $1.5 billion, the only option with a positive NPV of +$300MM
The attractive entry cost is driven by Player 2's distressed liquidation of assets following a rogue trader incident — this is a time-sensitive opportunity
This leaves approximately $1 billion of the $2.5 billion budget available for other passive investments
risks: Regulatory delays in acquiring the liquidated assets
Equities transaction volume is relatively low compared to Commodities and Options, limiting commission revenue upside
Equity markets are near all-time highs (2014 context); a future market correction would reduce transaction volumes and make profit projections overly optimistic
Client has no prior trading experience, creating operational and talent-acquisition risk
next_steps: Ascertain the process and timeline for acquiring Player 2's liquidated assets; determine whether other buyers are competing
Conduct due diligence on the specific assets (trading infrastructure, licenses, client relationships) being sold
Identify passive or low-attention investment opportunities for the remaining ~$1 billion in capital
Develop a talent acquisition plan given the client's lack of direct trading experience
